metadata.file_name: Brit J of Edu Psychol - 2023 - Pan - Using machine learning to predict UK and Japanese secondary students  life.pdf
metadata.title: Using machine learning to predict UK and Japanese secondary students' life satisfaction in PISA 2018

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 student questionnaire and well-being questionnaire data for the United Kingdom and Japan, with life satisfaction as the dependent variable. The analytic sample is restricted to students with non-missing values for the included variables, and missingness (<10%) is handled via series-mean imputation before model training. The manuscript does not report applying PISA complex survey weights (e.g., student/sampling weights) or replicate weights, and it instead focuses on ML model development and nested cross-validation. Because Random Forest and KNN are trained on preprocessed feature matrices, the paper’s weighting strategy is not documented; analysts should treat the results as predictive associations rather than population-representative estimates unless weights are confirmed in the original PISA microdata workflow.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values handling is not applicable because the dependent variable is life satisfaction derived from the PISA 2018 student questionnaire scale (0–10) rather than a PV-based cognitive achievement score. Missing data handling is reported: the authors state that missing values (<10%) were handled by imputing the series mean, so a PV-combining or PV-specific missing-data strategy is not required.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Students from the United Kingdom and Japan were selected from PISA 2018. The dependent variable is life satisfaction (ST016Q01NA) from the PISA 2018 student questionnaire, and the model uses 26 individual-level questionnaire/well-being variables listed in Table 2. Missing values for included variables were imputed using series mean (missingness <10%); the authors also report missing patterns in Appendix A (Table A1). No additional grade, school-type, or item-completion restrictions are described beyond using the extracted UK and Japan samples and imputing missing values.

top_predictors: ICT resources at home and school (ICTRES)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest (RF) — Test R2: 0.187 (mean across 5 outer folds), MSE: 0.203, RMSE: 0.451, MAE: 0.408. KNN — Test R2: 0.103, MSE: 0.224, RMSE: 0.474, MAE: 0.433.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Life satisfaction data for UK secondary students, the study leveraged Meaning in life, Motivation to master tasks, Student competition, ICT resources, and Exposure to bullying to predict life satisfaction, finding that the Random Forest model outperformed KNN on the UK data (higher test R2 and lower error). This indicates that strengthening meaning-in-life supports, managing competitive classroom climates, and improving ICT resources and anti-bullying efforts may be promising levers for improving students' subjective well-being, though the results are correlational due to the cross-sectional design.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest (RF) — Test R2: 0.138 (mean across 5 outer folds), MSE: 0.215, RMSE: 0.464, MAE: 0.434. KNN — Test R2: 0.055, MSE: 0.236, RMSE: 0.486, MAE: 0.451.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Life satisfaction data for Japan secondary students, the study leveraged Student cooperation, Self-efficacy, Meaning in life, Student competition, and Teacher support to predict life satisfaction, finding that the Random Forest model outperformed KNN on the Japanese data (higher test R2 and lower error). This indicates that policies and school practices that foster cooperative peer norms, build students' self-efficacy, and enhance teacher support may help improve life satisfaction, while also recognizing that the model captures predictive associations rather than causal effects.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2018 student questionnaire and well-being questionnaire data to predict secondary students’ life satisfaction (ST016Q01NA) separately for the United Kingdom and Japan. Two supervised ML regression models—Random Forest and k-nearest neighbours (KNN)—were trained using 26 individual-level predictors and evaluated with nested cross-validation (five outer folds, five inner folds) and grid-search hyperparameter tuning. Missing values (<10%) were handled by series-mean imputation, and performance was assessed with MSE, RMSE, MAE, and R². Across both countries, Random Forest performed better than KNN: for the UK, test R² was 0.187 (RF) vs 0.103 (KNN), and for Japan, 0.138 (RF) vs 0.055 (KNN). The most important predictors included meaning in life, student competition/cooperation, teacher support, exposure to bullying, and ICT resources, but the findings are correlational (cross-sectional questionnaire data) and the paper does not document the use of PISA complex survey weights.
